newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Sugar-No activity seen as China exits market.
newsitem.headline: Asian Sugar-No activity seen as China exits market.

text.p: Far East sugar traders were bemoaning a quiet market on Wednesday and said a lack of fundamental demand, especially from China, would dampen regional activity well through the first half of 1997.
"China is absolutely quiet -- and will stay this way," a trader in Hong Kong said.

Government restrictions on sugar imports for both consumption and tolling would remove a major factor from the international market -- one that could have hit 1.5 million tonnes worth of imports for 1997, sources said.
Tolling -- importing raw sugar and exporting the processed product -- was also restricted, another Hong Kong source said. Licences were necessary and excuses had better be good, he said.
China's taste for sugar is fickle, a Chinese trader said.
"When there is sugar available, Chinese people will eat it," he said. "When there's no sugar around, they won't and they won't miss it. It is not a necessary commodity in China."
This meant the government could afford another crackdown on the industry, in the hope of curtailing the massive losses faced year after year by processors, and wiping out smuggling and speculation.
Beijing's State Statistical Bureau reported on Monday that China produced 8.4 million tonnes of sugar in 1996, up 13.15 percent from 1995.
Traders polled by Reuters on Wednesday were sceptical about the official claim, suggesting production of 6.6 million tonnes would be closer to reality.
Chinese annual demand is generally put at eight to nine million tonnes.
Stocks have been built up since a crackdown on smuggling and tax evasion in 1995, and up to 400,000 tonnes of raw sugar is expected to arrive from Cuba this year, trading sources said.

There was no doubt among sugar trading sources that China would not be buying for at least the first half of 1997. One trader suggested China could announce before mid-year that there would be no imports in the second half either.
Domestic prices remained too low to justify any imports, for either consumption or tolling, sources said.
They quoted prices in Guangxi province, a major producing region, of 3,800 to 3,900 yuan (US$458-470) a tonne, and in Fujian of 4,000 yuan ($419).
Prices should go up to around 4,400 yuan ($530) a tonne before the summer months, one trader said, "because the carrying charges (interest, storage, transport) start to add up".
Other markets in Asia, notably South Korea, Malaysia and Japan, were covered, traders said. One source said South Korea bought one or two cargoes last week, but this could not be confirmed.
Japanese traders said premiums for January/March delivery were quoted at 0.70/0.75 cents (bid/offer) per pound over New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on an FOB basis.
March/May deliveries were quoted at 0.35/0.40 cents on the New York exchange, they said.
The Thai premiums on March deliveries eased slightly against last week, due to the expected arrival of Cuban sugar, traders said.
A source in Hong Kong said he expected premiums to fall further, below 30 cents and possibly closer to 20 "now that China is out of the picture".

Nissho Iwai Corp officials said last week that there was no problem with Cuban sugar shipments to Japan, clearing earlier concerns among traders that Nissho Iwai was covering raw sugar in Thailand to cope with expected delays in Cuban deliveries.
(US$1 = 8.3 yuan)
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6470
-- Eiichiro Tokumoto, Tokyo commodities desk (813) 3432 7391
